launches.tagline: Dream makes pocket-sized, battery-powered AI cameras that catch damage teams miss.
launches.body:
Hey everyone 👋, we are Ryland and Alexander, co-founders of Dream.

**TL;DR: Dream automatically photographs every vehicle or machine that passes through your gate, builds a 3D condition record, and uses AI to catch new damage the moment an asset passes through.**

**Launch Video: [https://youtu.be/uMP12lCb12E](https://youtu.be/uMP12lCb12E)**

**The problem**

Damage is an expensive leak for anyone who moves large, expensive assets in and out all day. It shows up two different ways:

**Car dealership service departments**

* As a car pulls into the service entrance, damage that could be identified and fixed goes unnoticed, which is lost revenue.
* Without a record of the car's condition on arrival, disputes come down to the customer's word against the dealership's, and the dealership gets blamed for pre-existing damage.

**High-value asset rentals (heavy equipment, trucks, boats, planes, trailers)**

* Teams are inconsistent about photographing assets as they go out and come back, so new damage gets missed before the customer is billed.
* When damage is missed, there's no evidence to charge the customer, so the company eats the repair cost out of pocket.

**What Dream does**

Dream cameras sit at your gate, lane, or service drive and turn every pass into evidence, automatically:

* **Continuous capture:** every vehicle or machine that moves through is photographed from every angle. No one has to remember to do it.
* **Asset identification:** Dream knows exactly what you need to look at.
* **3D reconstruction:** every pass becomes a complete 3D condition record for that asset.
* **AI damage detection:** on return or intake, Dream compares against the last record and flags new dents, scrapes, and visible changes right away.

The result is one clear source of truth for every asset's condition over time: rental companies catch damage before they bill so they stop eating repair costs, and dealership service departments find more fixable damage and resolve customer disputes with evidence.

Works across cars, vans, trucks, heavy equipment, and more.

**Why us**

We have spent years training models for aerial imaging and edge computer vision devices. Ryland has worked on the exact problem of detecting damage to assets from aerial imaging, such as degraded paint. Alexander has trained models that run on edge cameras deployed in the wild in Africa and India to detect poachers.

**Our ask**

We're onboarding partners now. **We'd love intros to:**

* **Car dealerships**
* **High-value asset rental companies** (heavy equipment, trucks, boats, planes, trailers)

If you run one of these, or know someone who does, please message us on LinkedIn!

launches.tagline: Making the physical world machine-readable across the entire electromagnetic spectrum
launches.body:
**TL;DR:** We are building a new kind of camera that can see through walls using radio waves. We provide construction, industrial inspection, and security teams with an accurate map of hidden objects behind walls and composite surfaces.

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2iEHRvcKN8g>

## **The Problem**

Most of the built world is opaque.

Pipes, cables, and structural elements hide behind walls until they're discovered mid-project, driving $20B+ a year in avoidable rework.

Defects remain hidden inside composites until parts break.

Entry teams are missing critical information before they breach a barrier.

## **The Solution**

An imaging platform that uses radio waves to see behind walls. It works just like a camera, requiring no training and producing high-resolution images that are instantly understandable. The resulting point cloud is natively to scale, accurate down to 1mm.

## **The Team**

Four engineers who've worked together for 8+ years, shipped multiple zero-to-one hardware products, and hold 250+ patents.

**Bilgehan** — PhD in electromagnetics; led antenna technologies on four iPhone generations, shipping the first phones with UWB and 5G mmWave; inventor of the zirconia dielectric resonator antenna.

**Brian** — built the earliest iPhone prototypes at Apple, co-invented iPhone multitouch and the Nest Learning Thermostat; degrees in Electrical and Civil Engineering.

**George** — MIT physicist; built x-ray imagers, retinal implants, optical sensors and the world's smallest laser projector.

**Paul** — Berkeley Mech.E.; ex-Apple and Humane product design lead; co-invented iPhone haptic Touch ID, IPX8 sealing.

## **What we built**

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=108275&key=user_uploads/2724984/c00b3438-c7f7-433f-941d-e021791e51c5)

We've built the hardware and imaging algorithms that can see behind composite layers and common building materials (sheetrock, tiles, marble, quartz, brick and insulation). Next step is our handheld platform that fuses our radio imaging with RGB and thermal cameras.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=108275&key=user_uploads/2724984/f1cf1ffa-8b23-4780-b363-13b0db90832d)

## **Our Ask**

We're looking for intros to decision makers at general contracting firms and industrial inspection teams, and to contacts with military access who can introduce and demo our systems to US defense organizations.

launches.title: Datost - The most accurate AI data analyst
launches.tagline: A proactive AI data analyst with a built in semantic layer that actually understands your business
launches.body:
Hey everyone — This is Maceo and Jason, founders of Datost.

**TL;DR:** Datost is an AI data analyst your team @mentions in Slack. It keeps a semantic layer of your business definitions so it understands what questions mean before writing SQL. On the hardest public text-to-SQL benchmark, it scores 75.2%. The best frontier model alone gets 33%.

**Why I built this**

We saw the problem while I was at Traba, a staffing marketplace. Traba had a lot of data and not enough analysts. Someone would need a number to make a decision, and the path to that number ran through SQL they couldn’t write or an analyst who was busy. The question would sit for hours. By the time the answer showed up, the decision had already been made on a guess.

There are AI analytics tools out there now. They all have the same problem: they don’t understand your business. When your PM asks “which accounts are at risk of churning,” there’s no column called that. “At risk” has a formula that lives in someone’s head, or a doc, or nowhere. These tools guess an interpretation and commit. Then someone in a Slack thread acts on the answer before anyone checks whether it was right.

**The semantic layer**

Datost maintains a layer of your team’s definitions, what “churn risk” means at your company, how you calculate NRR, which tables are trustworthy, what that internal acronym stands for.

When it hits a term it hasn’t seen, it looks it up the same way a new analyst would ask a coworker. When the semantic layer doesn’t have it either, it asks the user before writing any SQL.

It learns from mistakes too. When it gets something wrong, it leaves notes on the schema so it doesn’t make the same mistake twice. Teams that have been using it for a few months barely correct it anymore.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=99800&key=user_uploads/3433862/f456e145-3c20-47ed-b570-06e70b3c6cda)

**What it actually does**

Your team @mentions Datost in any Slack channel. It searches the semantic layer, explores your schema in a sandbox, writes and tests SQL, then posts the answer in-thread with the work shown. A second model reviews every answer read-only. If the definition says one thing and the SQL does another, the reviewer catches it.

It also runs on its own. You can set it up to post a pipeline coverage update to #sales every Monday, or flag when a metric moves outside a range you care about. Or if youre old fashioned it can make a beautiful dashboard for you :)

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=99800&key=user_uploads/3433862/f5c22b08-a608-47cd-a986-785487b6935e)

It connects to Postgres, MySQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks. Also Datadog, Sentry, PostHog, Coda, Notion, GitHub, and anything else via MCP. It reads your Slack history to see how things were answered before. It reads your codebase to understand how a metric is actually calculated. Charts, dashboards, PDFs, exports, whatever format you need. Most answers come back in under a minute.

**The benchmark**

We ran Datost against BIRD-Interact, the hardest public text-to-SQL benchmark. 600 deliberately ambiguous questions across 22 messy and realistic PostgreSQL databases, published at ICLR 2026. Every question uses terms that aren’t in the schema.

Claude Opus 4.6, the model Datost runs on, gets 33% on its own. Datost scored 75.2%. Same model. The gap is the semantic layer. On analytical questions, 91%.

Full breakdown here: <https://datost.com/blog/bird-interact>

**Ask**

If your team has a Slack, Teams, or Google Chat workspace and data people keep asking about, we can get you running in a day.

* [**Book a call**](https://datost.cal.com/founders/30-min)
* Email me or Jason: [maceo@datost.com](mailto:maceo@datost.com) or [jason@datost.com](mailto:jason@datost.com)  
* Or reply here

Modern warfare, however, demands wide-area, persistent coverage that is both passive and economically scalable. By utilising a mesh architecture, Arlo Industries unlocks unprecedented asymmetric economics. The network is fundamentally built to scale: the cost of adding sensors grows linearly, but the tracking accuracy increases exponentially, delivering highly resilient, persistent coverage for a fraction of the cost of legacy systems.

Deo founded Arlo Industries after spending over 6 years in the Israeli defence ecosystem, where he lived through multiple conflicts and experienced the Iron Dome and other systems in action against ICBMs and the infamous Shahed drones. launches.tagline: We build sensors that track drones & missiles better than radars
launches.body:
---

**Hi, I'm Deo, founder of [Arlo Industries](https://arlo1.com/).**

<https://youtu.be/2F0cugbrq3A>

**The problem**

Modern air defence depends on active radars: expensive, emitting, and targetable. A single ground-based radar unit can cost tens of millions, broadcasts its location to anything listening, and leaves massive coverage gaps against low-altitude threats like drones.

This architecture was built for a different era. Today's threat, swarms of cheap drones and cruise missiles flying below radar coverage, exploits every weakness of centralised, active sensing.

**What we're building**

Mentat is a passive, distributed sensing network.

* **Tracks aerial objects in 3D without emitting**: invisible to the threats it detects
* **Accurately track smaller threats**: our mesh works together to better pinpoint small targets
* **Scales via many low-cost nodes**: instead of a few high-value targets, we employ asymmetric economics where adding nodes grows linearly in cost but tracking accuracy increases exponentially

We're the sensing layer, the force multiplier for every interceptor and C-UAS system in the market.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=101954&key=user_uploads/836806/ddbe92c9-897d-4e52-90ab-c8574ed7335c)

**What we're really building**

Drone detection is our wedge, not our ceiling. The real innovation isn't in any single sensor, it's in the network that ties it all together. We're building the foundational sensing and communications infrastructure layer for frontline defence. A distributed, resilient network that future defence technologies will plug into. Like the **Starlink before the Starship.**

**Why now**

Low-altitude airspace is increasingly contested. Ukraine, Nordics, Eastern Europe, & Middle East, operators everywhere are discovering that the cost curve of traditional radar doesn't scale against distributed drone threats. At the same time, edge compute, distributed systems, and passive optical sensing have reached the point where a fundamentally different architecture is viable.

**Backstory**

I spent 6+ years in Israel, living through multiple conflicts and seeing systems like Iron Dome operate against ballistic missiles and drones firsthand. When a Shahed drone exploded near my apartment, the gap between what exists and what's needed became personal. Since then, I've been in Ukraine and across Eastern Europe, working directly with military operators and validating in real conflict environments.

📍Field Test - Ukraine

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=101954&key=user_uploads/836806/b380d961-dde4-4e50-b6eb-1cbf708e6d3c)

**Traction**

* Active technology demonstrations with Ukrainian military on the frontlines
* Partnerships and military relationships across USA, Ukraine, Finland, and Estonia.
* Team includes a PhD in drones/autonomy and military domain experts

**Our asks**

launches.title: Edgerun: The 10 lb Military Exoskeleton
launches.tagline: Powered exoskeleton that assists every step a soldier takes under combat load
launches.body:
**TL;DR:** Edgerun builds powered legs for soldiers. A 10 lb exoskeleton worn at the waist that adds assistance to every step and cuts the effort of moving under a combat load by 30-45%. Since May, we've run 100+ field tests with Ukrainian operators out of our Kyiv field office.

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nFLeQV2DWMc>

**▍The problem**

Every system on the modern battlefield has been upgraded. The human carrying it has not.

* For 2,500 years the soldier's load sat around 40 lbs. In the last 40 years it **doubled, then doubled again**.
* A US infantryman now carries **90-140 lbs** into a fight. The Army's own field manual sets the limit at 48 lbs.
* On deployment, load carriage causes **twice as many** evacuations as enemy contact.
* The Pentagon and VA spend **$9.3B a year** on the injuries it leaves behind.

Battles are won through speed and surprise. Load kills both.

**▍Why now**

Sixty years of military exoskeletons died the same death. The device cost more to carry than it gave back. SOCOM's TALOS burned $400M before it was cancelled in 2019.

That all changed in the last 18 months. The humanoid robotics boom produced one-pound actuators that put out 30+ Nm of torque, and 21700 cells crossed 450 Wh/kg. The components finally exist. They’re getting better every quarter.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=112214&key=user_uploads/1393855/cd255b24-3429-4270-9670-e28fc8df360b)

**▍What we built**

Our first exoskeleton is a bilateral hip system worn at the waist. It reads your gait in real time and adds torque at the moment your hip drives forward. The hip produces about 60% of the force in loaded walking, so assisting it gives the most help-per-pound of anything you could strap to the body.

* Under 10 lbs with batteries
* 30-45% less metabolic cost under a combat load
* On in 5 seconds, off in one
* 12+ hours on hot-swappable drone-class batteries
* Quasi-direct-drive actuators, composite structures, CAN bus. Nothing exotic by design.

The soldier arrives at the objective still able to fight, patrols 10 km farther, and keeps a body that lasts past one tour.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=112214&key=user_uploads/1393855/94bf48a9-0ba6-4ce7-94a2-f467cae9657c)

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=112214&key=user_uploads/1393855/883d1e98-900a-420a-b7ff-e56cc8911c0c)

**▍Ukraine**

Our field engineers work out of a Kyiv office, alongside operators from infantry, special operations, and National Guard units who provide structured feedback every day. [Balistyka](https://balistyka.ua/), one of Ukraine's leading body armor makers, is an integration partner, helping us ensure our system fits the kit soldiers already wear.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=112214&key=user_uploads/1393855/89a30d39-fe11-421c-abe7-32961da8d1bd)

**▍The mission**

Defense is the first customer, not the last. Read the mission at edgerun.com/mission

name: Egoist Machines
long_description:
Egoist Machines is building infrastructure for a world where your personal context belongs to you, rather than to the apps and AI companies you use. Today, every assistant and consumer app builds its own version of you. We think that architecture is backwards. Your context should live with you, persist across products, and be available to any model, app or agent you choose.

AI Passport is the first layer of that infrastructure. It brings the context you generate across AI assistants and everyday apps into one portable profile you control. Tell ChatGPT something and Claude can already know it, for example. Switch to a new product and it can understand you from the first interaction, without the new company needing to own the underlying data.

Apps integrate through Sign in with AI Passport, requesting only the context they need for a specific purpose and duration. Users can see what is being accessed and revoke that access later. Underneath, we have built our own memory infrastructure for fast, compact per-user retrieval and permissioned access.

We are distributing AI Passport directly to consumers through first-party products, while integrating it into consumer applications with existing distribution. Every new product that uses Passport gives users another reason to maintain their context there, and every additional Passport holder makes the context layer more useful to developers.

The next step is to build a true Egoist Machine: an intelligent system whose memory, incentives and actions are governed by the individual it represents. We call it Digital Domovoy, the hardware extension of AI Passport. Instead of your most personal context ultimately living on somebody else's servers, it lives and is processed locally on hardware you control. AI Passport becomes the permission layer between that private local context and the cloud models and internet services you choose to use.

Our North Star is the Egoist Machine: an intelligent system whose memory, incentives and actions are governed by the individual it represents.

launches.title: Egoist Machines: user-owned hyper-personalisation infrastructure for Web 4.0
launches.tagline: One portable, permissioned memory and context layer for hyper-personalisation across every AI application.
launches.body:
**TL;DR:** We are building AI Passport, the user-owned context layer for consumer AI. It lets people carry their personal context between products while controlling exactly what each product can access, why, and for how long.

Read our manifesto for the bigger vision: <https://ego.ist/notes/the-egoist-machine>

Create your AI Passport to start taking control of your data: <https://ego.ist/>

**Ask**: if you’re working on a consumer-facing AI application, or know someone who is, we’d love to chat: [founders@ego.ist](mailto:founders@ego.ist)

<https://youtu.be/nLnZNjyHV0s>

The next era of consumer technology will be **hyper-personalised**. The products that understand each user from the very first interaction will create fundamentally better experiences and, we believe, the next consumer decacorns. People increasingly lack the time and patience to train every new product from scratch.

The main blocker to ubiquitous consumer AI is that every major AI assistant and consumer app is building its own private and incomplete model of the same person. ChatGPT holds one model, Claude another, while the data in health apps, calendar, shopping history, travel accounts, wearables, and financial tools remain trapped in separate silos. No product has the complete context needed to understand you, and no user has a single place from which to control it.

As a result:

\- Users get bored of repeatedly explaining themselves;

\- Companies spend money building context that already exists;

\- Personal data remains trapped inside platforms the user does not control.

The natural end state of this inefficiency is one user-owned memory and context layer that sits above individual products. Apps request the specific context they need, and users grant scoped, time-limited access instead of permanently surrendering their data.

**_That is AI Passport_**.

---

## How AI Passport works

AI Passport is a centralised, user-controlled home for personal context.

You can think of it as **Link for personal context**. Link lets people securely save their payment and shipping information once and reuse it across businesses; AI Passport does the same for _all_ your context, including preferences, interests, goals, history, health, travel, and so much more.

Users bring this context into one centralised AI Passport by connecting the apps and AI assistants they already use. They can also save anything they discover online or on social media directly to their Passport. New information enters an approval inbox, where the user decides whether it becomes _private memory_ or part of their _living, shareable public profile_.

That same Passport then becomes a plug-and-play connector for consumer apps through our **Sign in with AI Passport** OAuth system:

1\. An app requests the specific context it needs.

2\. The user sees exactly what is being requested, why it is needed, and how long access will last.

3\. The user can approve, edit, or deny the request, with the option to grant one-time, time-limited, or continuing access .

4\. Every permission can later be inspected or revoked.

We are launching AI Passport directly to consumers and through distribution and deep-integration partners collectively reaching millions of users across dining, ride-hailing, wearables, healthcare, lifestyle, finance and more.

We built a custom memory backend for AI Passport. It is optimised for compact, exact retrieval across isolated per-user memory stores and supports cryptographic access control at the memory layer. The retrieval path is constrained by the user's active permission, so the product can access only the context authorised for that purpose and period.

---

## Who we are

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=111045&key=user_uploads/3328552/4bb1bba6-8c9f-4d94-b88a-28051f5e6e45)

**Dr David Khachaturov** holds a PhD (Uni of Cambridge) in Computer Science and is the youngest-ever Fellow at St Catharine's College, Cambridge. Previously an ML Researcher at OpenAI (PaperBench) and Lead AI Security Researcher at FrontierOne.

**Erin Meryl McGurk** grew 0 to 1M followers on socials in one year. Advised Uni of Cambridge, UK Govt, OpenAI on social media strategy. Founded social enterprise Girl Economics to 15 countries, 75 ambassadors, 10+ weekly events.

---

## Our Ask

**For users:** create your AI Passport (<https://ego.ist>) and tell us what you think!

**For builders:** if you are building a product that could benefit from richer user context, explore our developer docs (<https://ego.ist/docs>) and feel free to reach out to [founders@ego.ist](mailto:founders@ego.ist).

We would especially value introductions to teams building consumer AI, wearables, health products, commerce experiences, or agents that need bounded access to sensitive personal information. If that is you, I want to chat: <https://calendar.app.google/qT5ccAUEqB9V82Uz9>

launches.tagline: Kara grows and engineers diamond wafers for thermal management, semiconductor and quantum applications
launches.body:
**TL;DR:** We grow high-purity diamond wafers for scientific and industrial applications. Our diamond thermal wafers can be used in aircraft, spacecraft, RF electronics, and lasers to move heat dramatically better than conventional materials. We’re helping hardware run cooler, faster, and more reliably with diamond that is 5× more thermally conductive than copper.

Here is a link to our launch video: 

<https://youtu.be/16aad1cU_FM>

**The Problem**

The world’s most valuable hardware systems are limited by how quickly they can remove heat.

For AI chips, that means expensive GPUs throttle and deliver less compute. In aircraft and satellites, it means carrying more cooling mass. In RF systems and lasers, it limits sustained output power.

Adding more cooling costs space, and energy, and sometimes is simply not possible.

**What We Built**

Diamond is usually something you wear. We make it something engineers can build with.

Diamond conducts heat up to **5× better than copper while weighing \~60% less** for the same volume. It is electrically insulating and stable in extreme environments.

Today we manufacture:

* Diamond heat spreaders for AI and high-performance computing
* Ultra-high-purity diamond wafers for thermal, photonic and quantum applications
* Diamond-metal composites (copper and aluminium) for thermal management
* Metallized and bondable diamond plates
* Custom-engineered diamond components

We are now producing custom samples under pilot agreements and purchase orders for thermal, electronic, aerospace, and quantum applications.

Silicon transformed computing when we learned to manufacture it with extreme purity and control. Kara is doing the same with diamond. Today, our ultra-high-purity diamond pulls heat away from silicon chips.

**Tomorrow, Kara’s control over purity and defects unlocks diamond as the ultimate semiconductor.**

**Why us**

[@Aarin Jhaveri](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/3669602) is a fifth-generation diamantaire who has sold millions of dollars in natural and lab-grown diamonds and worked across the supply chain.

[@Anuveer Chadha](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/3669310) is a chemical engineer who has worked on diamond quantum sensing and advanced-materials research at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory with the Department of Defense and Department of Energy.

Diamond is our unfair advantage. We know how to grow, control, and engineer it far beyond jewelry.

**Our ask**

**Today, we're looking for introductions to engineers building hardware that is limited by heat.** 

Specifically:

* AI accelerator packaging teams
* Advanced packaging / OSAT engineers
* Aerospace, space, and defence electronics
* Data-centre infrastructure companies
* High-power RF and GaN teams

Introduce us to the engineer responsible for the hottest, hardest-to-cool hardware, especially where size, weight, or power makes cooling difficult. 

We’ll build them a custom diamond sample to test.

Email us at [founders@karalabs.ai](mailto:founders@karalabs.ai) or book time here: <https://calendly.com/aarin-berkeley/aarin-jhaveri-s-calender>

**Diamond spent centuries as a symbol of “extraordinary”. We are making it something the world can build with.**

name: DeepReach Inc.
long_description:
Physical AI — robots and world models — is bottlenecked on one thing: diverse,
real-world data at massive scale showing how humans actually do work in the
physical world. It was never written down, and you can't buy it, because no one
has ever captured it. Only real local experts, the people who do this work every
day, can produce data this authentic and valuable.

DeepReach builds the network that reaches them. We design and manufacture
wearable stereo capture devices, then place them with local data partners who
run collection as their own business — in warehouses, workshops, farms, kitchens
and repair shops. They own the local relationships; we supply the hardware, the
software platform, the quality pipeline and the payments. Anyone can run a data
business.

That structure is what produces diversity. Instead of thousands of hours inside
one environment, we deliver hours spread across thousands of environments —
which is what actually makes robot policies generalize.

475 devices in the field and 100+ data partners are live across 7 countries, adding new
partners every week. They've collected nearly 150,000 clips in the past three
months, with volume roughly doubling month over month. Our data is in production
with multiple frontier model and robotics companies, and we're scaling to
10,000+ devices across 50 countries.
one_liner: Network for Physical AI Data Business

question_answers.question: How did your company get started? (i.e., How did the founders meet? How did you come up with the idea? How did you decide to be a founder?)
question_answers.answer:
Chris and I are from the same hometown and have known each other for ten years, long before either of us thought about robots.

In that time I built two companies around the same problem: how do you organize people you'll never meet, in places you'll never visit, to do consistent work? The first was HireIO, a cross-border staffing platform out of Silicon Valley. The second was Talex, an expert network for LLM data annotation — around 70,000 people across ten countries. Chris went the other direction: a CS PhD at USC in computer vision, ML infrastructure at Meta, then founding ML engineer at Aven.

Running an annotation network for language models, I kept hitting the same wall from the supply side. Text was running out, and the next generation of models wasn't going to learn from the internet. It was going to learn from the physical world — and nobody had captured it. What a warehouse picker, a line cook or a phone repair technician knows is real expertise, and none of it was ever written down. You can't buy that data, because it doesn't exist yet. Chris was hitting the same wall from the model side, watching what was missing from training sets.

The default answer at the time was to put a lab in one city and record thousands of hours in the same room. That produces volume, not diversity, and robot policies don't generalize from volume. What the models needed was the opposite shape: a few hours each from thousands of different real workplaces, all over the world. Which meant the bottleneck wasn't an AI problem. It was a distributed human network problem — reaching thousands of ordinary businesses across dozens of countries, and giving the people already working in them a reason to capture what they do. That was the problem I'd spent two companies learning to solve.

We started DeepReach in 2025. Chris owns perception and the data engine; I own the network, hardware operations and the commercial side. Ten years of knowing each other means we skipped most of the negotiation that takes co-founders their first year.

question_answers.question: What is the core problem you are solving? Why is this a big problem? What made you decide to work on it?
question_answers.answer:
Core problem: robot models can't generalize, because the data they learn from all looks the same.

Physical AI needs to see how work actually happens — a mechanic torquing a bolt, a baker shaping dough, a technician opening a phone. None of it was ever written down. The internet captured what people say about the world; it never captured how people act in it. So unlike language models, this generation can't be trained on scraped text. Every hour has to be collected on purpose. 

Today the field has roughly tens of thousands of hours of this data against a need estimated in the hundreds of millions. But the gap isn't really a volume gap. It's a diversity gap. The standard approach is to build a lab, hire operators, and record for months in one controlled space. That yields thousands of hours that all look alike, and a policy trained on it fails the moment the lighting, the counter height, or the tool changes. Our customers' acceptance specs now reflect this directly: they cap how much of a delivery can come from any single environment type, and reject batches that are too concentrated. Diversity is the binding constraint, and it's now contractual.

Diversity is hard for an economic reason, not a technical one. Collecting one hour each from a thousand real workplaces means negotiating access to a thousand real businesses — each with an owner who has no reason to let a stranger film their operation, in a country where you have no presence. That cost is why everyone else builds the lab instead. It's a distribution problem wearing an AI problem's clothes. \
\
That's why we built the company as a network rather than an operation. The people who already work in those places, and already have the trust and the access, run collection as their own local business. We give them the hardware, the software and the payments. Access stops being something we buy and becomes something the network already has. \
\
I decided to work on this from the supply side. I'd spent two companies building cross-border human networks — a staffing platform, then a 70,000-person annotation network across ten countries — and kept watching demand arrive for data that no existing structure could produce. The bottleneck was never the model. It was that nobody had built the network that reaches the physical world.

question_answers.question: What is your long-term vision? If you truly succeed, what will be different about the world?
question_answers.answer:
The long-term vision is a network that can reach any workplace on earth, and a record of how human work is actually done.

Concretely: 10,000+ devices, 50 countries, one million commercial scenes, ten million task types. Every deployment adds to what we call the Human Skill Library — a permanent record of how people do physical work, built from the inside by the people who do it. Much of this knowledge exists nowhere else. It lives in the hands of a mechanic who has been doing the job for thirty years, and when he retires it's gone. Text and video on the internet captured what people say about work. Nobody has captured the work. 

\
If we succeed, two things are different：\
First, robots stop being confined to the places that can afford to build around them. Today automation only pays at Amazon scale — a facility large enough to redesign itself for the machine. That's a rounding error of the world's actual workplaces. A policy trained on a million real environments doesn't need the environment to change; it works in a repair shop with bad lighting and a counter at the wrong height. That's the difference between robotics as a capability the largest companies buy and robotics as infrastructure a small business can use.\
Second, the people whose work teaches these models are inside the economy that results. The last generation of AI was trained on data scraped from people who were never asked and never paid. This one has to be collected on purpose, from real workers in real workplaces, which means it can be built the other way — as something people opt into and earn from. We already have data partners in ten countries running this as a business they own. At 10,000 operators that isn't a side effect of how we source data. It's the point.

launches.body:
**TL;DR:** DeepReach is a global data network that equips local entrepreneurs with wearable devices to capture the real-world operation data for Physical AI training. By decentralizing collections across thousands of entrepreneurs who have access to local businesses, they provide high-diversity training data that cannot be accessed elsewhere. DeepReach already signed multiple-million-dollar contracts with frontier AI labs.\
\
**DeepReach is building a global network for real-world human data to train Physical AI.**

We enable local entrepreneurs to operate data-collection businesses using our wearable capture devices, while we provide the hardware, software, QA, and customers.

The result is a distributed network that produces the diverse human demonstrations Physical AI labs cannot obtain anywhere else. Every new data partner expands the diversity and value of the network.

In just three months, DeepReach has helped **150+ entrepreneurs** build data businesses employing **1,000+ local experts** across **7 countries**. Together, they’ve collected **500,000+ real-world operation clips**, captured **150,000+ professional skill demonstrations**, and secured **several million dollars in customer contracts** with frontier AI labs and robotics companies.

▶ **Watch how it works:** <https://youtu.be/q5mLwju5Q8U?si=CT3FHbNJaIteNXZD>

---

# **The Problem**

Frontier AI is already learning from the physical world.

The challenge is no longer collecting data, it’s collecting **diverse** real-world data at scale.

Most companies solve this by building collection labs or hiring workers directly. Both approaches scale headcount, but neither scales access. The hardest part is reaching millions of real workplaces across different industries, countries, and working conditions.

Without that diversity, AI struggles to generalize beyond a small number of controlled environments.

---

# **What We Built**

Instead of building another data collection company, **we built a platform where entrepreneurs launch independent real-world data businesses.**

DeepReach provides the wearable devices, software platform, quality infrastructure, customer demand, operational support, and payments. **Entrepreneurs build and grow the businesses.**

They recruit local experts, develop trusted relationships with local businesses, and continuously expand into new industries, communities, and real-world environments.

**Every new business expands the platform’s reach into the physical world, creating access to places, people, and skills that centralized data collection simply can’t reach.**

The result isn’t a larger workforce, it’s **a growing ecosystem of independent data businesses** that continuously expands the world’s supply of diverse real-world data for Physical AI.

---

# **Where We Are**

In just three months:

* **150+ entrepreneurs** have launched data businesses on DeepReach
* Those businesses now employ **1,000+ local experts** across **7 countries**
* **500,000+ real-world operation clips** collected
* **150,000+ professional skill demonstrations** captured
* **Several million dollars in signed customer contracts** with frontier AI labs and robotics companies
* Scaling toward **10,000+ devices** across **20 countries**

# **Where This Goes**

Our model is simple: labs list the tasks and environments they need, our entrepreneurs pick up the orders and go record them, and every delivery makes the network more capable of fulfilling the next one. It also compounds into something bigger, what we call the **Human Skill Library**: a growing record of how people interact with the physical world.

Most of this knowledge has never been documented. It lives in the hands of experienced workers, passed down through practice rather than words, and it often disappears when they retire.

Our vision is to preserve and scale humanity's physical knowledge, so every AI system can learn from the collective experience of human work.

# **About Us**

\
Tim built HireIO into a leading global workforce company with 15 millions in annual revenue, then founded [Talex.ai](http://Talex.ai), an AI-powered expert network, before starting DeepReach. Chris comes from a computer vision background. We discovered the problem firsthand while labeling data for robotics startups: the real bottleneck wasn’t annotation, it was capturing diverse real-world human skills at scale.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=110389&key=user_uploads/1294315/9bb8c293-ab57-42aa-b756-58562e546b78)

---

# **How You Can Help**

If you’re building frontier AI systems and need more diverse real-world data, we’d love to talk.

If you’re an entrepreneur interested in building a real-world data business, applications are open here: [www.deepreach.ai/join](https://www.deepreach.ai/join)

Tim Li\
Founder & CEO, DeepReach AI

launches.body:
**TL;DR:** AI hardware trades over phone calls and forwarded spreadsheets. No venue, no price to mark against: lenders mark billions in GPU collateral off appraisals. We're building Stoa, an RFQ marketplace where buyers and sellers get firm quotes within 48 hours, and settled trades build the prices the market can mark, finance, and hedge against.

<https://youtu.be/zbD21BgAo88>

GPU deals close in group chats. We know because we've been in them.

A price arrives as a voice note. Someone forwards an inventory list, then it gets forwarded again, and soon three brokers are offering the same machines. Nobody knows who actually owns what or whether any quote is firm.

The market behind those chats is worth hundreds of billions of dollars a year. Lenders mark billions in GPU collateral off appraisals, not trades.

We're Berat, Eren, and Kaan. We're building Stoa.

AI hardware is becoming an asset class, but its market is missing the basics: a venue where hardware can trade, prices that buyers, sellers, and lenders can mark against, and eventually financing and hedging built on those prices. We're starting with the venue: an RFQ marketplace for GPUs. It gets buyers and sellers firm quotes, and every bid and settlement builds the history the rest needs.

**Here's how it works**

Post what you want to buy or sell: B300s, H200s, H100s, a bare card or a full cluster, new or secondary.

Vetted dealers bid blind with firm quotes. Instead of spending weeks calling around, you get through the RFQ in 48 hours.

We handle the unglamorous parts too: KYB and counterparty checks, contracts, shipping, and settlement.

In our first month, $300M+ in RFQs ran through the book.

**Why the marketplace comes first**

Ask what an H100 is worth and everyone you call gives you a different answer.

On Stoa, dealers quote against the same RFQ without seeing each other's bids. Because every RFQ, firm quote, award, and settlement runs through us, we see what the hardware actually trades for.

A quote is an opinion. A settled trade is a receipt.

That transaction history becomes prices buyers, sellers, and lenders can mark against. Once marks are grounded in settled trades, financing and hedging can follow.

Platts started printing oil prices in a magazine. Kelley Blue Book began as one dealer's published list of what he'd pay for cars. GPU inventory is still being passed around in forwarded spreadsheets, and Blackwell upgrades are now pushing H100 fleets into the secondary market.

Someone is going to be the price.

**The team**

We've known each other for more than ten years. We have founded companies, traded interest rate derivatives, and built trading and pricing infrastructure for oil and gas. Now we're building it for AI hardware.

**Buying or selling?**

If you're buying GPUs or compute, or you're sitting on hardware, sign up at [stoaexchange.com](http://stoaexchange.com).

**Schedule a call: [https://stoa.cal.com/stoa/intro](https://stoa.cal.com/stoa/intro)**

And if you know infrastructure heads at neoclouds or data centers, hyperscaler capex teams, dealers, ITADs, or credit desks lending against GPUs, please send this their way.

Berat, Eren & Kaan

**What if you could hire a robot the same way you hire a temp worker?** 

Nick grew up working in his family’s 3rd-generation distribution business, where he saw firsthand how much warehouses still depend on manual labor. The obvious answer should have been robotics, but for true labor replacement, existing robots were too expensive, inflexible, and difficult to deploy. As a result, most warehouses still say they’re “not ready” for automation.

Nick came together with his best friend Josh, a fellow UPenn alum and PhD at Caltech specializing in safety-critical control for robotics, to solve this problem.

Manifold is building robotic labor for the supply chain industry. Its robots perform picking jobs from start to finish faster than humans, with no upfront cost or infrastructure changes. Customers simply pay per pick, at a cost below human labor.

They’re already deploying robots to perform more than **5 million picks across multiple warehouses.**

name: Nori
long_description:
We manufacture Nori: A sub-$2000 bimanual mobile manipulator that can clean rooms, restock shelves, and fold clothes. Nori can handle basic tasks out of the box, and its software lets anyone teach Nori to automate work specific to their home or business. 

Nori aims to solve the robotics data bottleneck. By deploying affordable robots to customers around the world, we can gather the diverse data required to train the next generation of generalist robotic policies. Every user of Nori makes Nori smarter.

Since launching 6 weeks ago we have already deployed our first robot and have over $440k+ in sales.

We can bring general-purpose robotics to homes and businesses that could never afford it before. There are 132.7 million households and 8.4 million employer business locations in the U.S. At $1,688 per robot, selling just one Nori to 0.5% of them represents a $1.2B market opportunity in the U.S. alone.
one_liner: The most capable American-made humanoid robot for $1,688

question_answers.question: What is the core problem you are solving? Why is this a big problem? What made you decide to work on it?
question_answers.answer:
Robots are finally capable enough to be useful, but they're priced like cars, not appliances. A capable humanoid costs $20,000+, so general-purpose robots stay in labs and pilots instead of homes. 

It's a big problem because household labor is one of the largest unpriced markets in the world. Today's answer is a stack of single-task machines, a dishwasher, a washer, a vacuum, each $600 to $1,000 and doing exactly one thing. Whoever ships a general-purpose robot at appliance prices doesn't win a niche, they open consumer robotics the way the PC opened computing.

We're robotics researchers from Columbia (RoboPIL, CGUI). After years watching \[$100K research robots struggle with tasks cheap hardware could handle\], we realized the gap between lab robots and home robots isn't intelligence, it's cost discipline. Nobody was going to fix that from inside a lab, so we left to build it: a $1,688 robot anyone can teach.

launches.title: Risklytics: Insurance for the Frontier
launches.tagline: Insurance for companies pushing the frontier of what is possible with AI, from robot fleets to agents in production.
launches.body:
**TLDR:** Risklytics is a commercial insurance brokerage for companies building with AI in the physical space, from robot fleets on customer sites to agents running in production. This year many insurance companies stopped covering risks that involve AI. We find the insurers that will still cover it, translate what you're building into terms they can price, and read every clause before anything is signed.

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jHTzpKbmZa4>

**The problem**

Starting this year, many insurance companies began excluding coverage for injury and property damage arising out of AI.

For a hardtech company that language reaches everything you do. If AI touched the work anywhere, including the tools your engineers designed it with or the product itself, the insurer can deny the claim.

The problem with these exclusions is that they get added account by account, so the same hardware can be covered at one insurer and excluded at the next, and nothing in the process makes that obvious. It shows up as a form number on the endorsement list attached to your renewal, which is why most founders don't learn they have one until they file a claim.

**Why now**

Physical AI is scaling faster than the insurance market underneath it. Insurance moves slower, and its first instinct with an unfamiliar risk is to exclude it and wait for loss data. Cyber went the same way: exclusions first, then specialists who understood it, then a real market. AI is at the exclusion stage now, and these companies pushing the frontier can't wait for the cycle to finish on its own. 

**What we do**

We handle the whole coverage process end to end.

You send us an application. We take what you're building and put it in terms an insurance company can understand and price.

Then we go to market. We have access to hundreds of insurance companies, the ones that actually write this kind of risk, and we take your file to them. Most will pass. The few that want it compete on price and terms, and we keep shopping until every requirement you have is met, including the limits your customer contracts demand.

When offers come back we read the policies line by line. If an AI exclusion is attached, we push to get it removed, or we find a company that writes the AI coverage in on purpose. Then we tell you in plain terms what you've got.

We cover the lines your company actually needs: general liability, umbrella, property, equipment in transit and on customer sites, workers' comp, professional liability, management liability, and cyber.

You never pay us. The insurance company pays us a commission out of the premium when a policy is placed, so applying costs you nothing and there's no additional fee from us at any point.

**Where this goes**

Physical AI is expanding faster than any industry, and every company in it buys insurance every year for as long as it exists. The programs grow as the fleets grow.

We want to be the brokerage that grows with them: the people who know this risk best, hold the relationships with the markets that write it, and build the loss data of the future.

**Why us**

We're Sam and Alex, on leave from Harvard. We were already in insurance building models when we noticed that batch mates building some of the most innovative technology in the world couldn't get covered at all. Since then we’ve landed partnerships to offer these frontier companies easier access to better policies.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=110197&key=user_uploads/2666435/74c5c462-a2ff-44b8-ac6c-f8ebc7807dbd)


**The ask**

If you're building anything on the frontier, apply at[ risklytics.ai](http://risklytics.ai). It takes a few minutes, it costs nothing, and we'll come back with what the market says.

It doesn't matter what you have in place today. If you're building, we want to get you covered.

And if you're an insurer, MGA or wholesaler with appetite here, we want to talk:[ risklytics.ai/markets](https://www.risklytics.ai/markets/)

name: Ultrasonium
long_description:
The technologies that define this century, including data centers, rockets, satellites, and robots, are built from complex metal parts. As these systems advance, the parts get harder to make. Past a certain complexity, casting and machining stop working, and the advanced methods that remain are slow, expensive, and hazardous.

Ultrasonium has invented a new manufacturing method to make these critical parts 15x faster and 75% cheaper than the methods they replace, in the U.S. and at scale. Solid metal feedstock goes in and a finished part safely comes out, controlled by a physical AI layer and novel control processes. 

The systems that matter most, in aerospace, energy, and compute, are demanding metal geometries that can't be machined or cast and are too expensive and slow to make with incumbent methods, at a moment when domestic manufacturing capacity is a national priority.

Our founding team has built and innovated some of the most complex engineering systems known to man: quantum computers, superconductors, nuclear reactors, and novel aerospace alloy processing methods.

launches.title: Lamb Labs: Custom Chips for AI Inference
launches.tagline: Co-designed models and silicon: we hardcode the model architecture into chips targeting 20,000+ tokens per second and 63x higher intelligence per watt.
launches.body:
**Hi Everyone!** 

**We’re Niki and Thomas - cofounders of Lamb Labs.**  

**TL;DR: We build custom AI inference chips that run inference at 20,000+ tok/s and 63x higher intelligence per watt than a traditional GPU. Fully local and private by construction, no subscriptions, no API costs.** 

**Our mission: the world’s fastest LLM at the lowest power.** 

<https://youtu.be/MhhY1Dy9ltE?feature=shared>

**Our hot take: AI models are finally getting good enough to hardcode them directly into silicon.** Once you stop treating the chip as a general-purpose GPU and burn a specific model into hardware, inference gets radically faster and cheaper per watt. Most of the industry is still building flexible, general chips. We think that flexibility is exactly what's wasting your energy. So we’re on a mission to reduce the energy footprint of AI. 

**The Problem**

AI is taking power on two fronts: concentrating control of data and intelligence, and consuming ever more electricity to grow. That future scares us, so we're building against it.

Here's the technical root of the waste: **GPUs burn most of their energy during inference moving data, not computing.** LLM/VLM inference is memory-bound, fetching a weight from memory costs \~100–1000x the energy of the arithmetic you do with it. So you underutilize the GPU you paid for: some GPUs only hit 20–40% compute utilization during LLM inference while the rest idles waiting on memory.

Cloud hosting adds its own tax: expensive per-token bills, latency you can't control, network dependencies, and your data leaving your control.

**Our Solution**

We build the model and the chip together. 

The Hardware Layer

* **Custom architecture, RL-tuned.** We built an RL environment that co-designs the chip architecture for a given model, optimizing directly for speed and energy per token.
* **Aggressive quantization.** Removes complex math, which shrinks the size and cost of the chip.
* **Weights on-chip.** The model weights live where the compute is overcoming the memory-bandwidth bottleneck

 

Because everything is hardcoded, it's fully local and secure by construction. No connectivity dependency, nothing leaves the device.

The Software Layer 

Designing the chip led us to solving a fundamental flaw in LLMs so we are now open-sourcing a new model next week, converted from another open source model, to run 2x faster on any hardware. Come back next week for part 2 of our launch to find out more….

**Our Ask**

If you answer "yes" to any of these, we'd love your help:

* **Are you paying for inference in watts, not just dollars?** Neocloud or private DC operators who are power- or hardware-cost-bound rather than demand-bound, talk to us.
* **Do you need inference where the cloud isn't an option?** Private AI deployments, regulated, air-gapped, sovereign, or bandwidth-starved deployments.

name: Robocurve
long_description:
Robocurve builds open-source tools and independent benchmarks to measure how well robots can do real-world jobs. Instead of relying on unverified demo videos from frontier labs, we score their models on reproducible benchmarks that anyone can trust.

Today there are no well-run, standardized robotics benchmarks. Labs evaluate in-house, and no independent group has stepped in to run continuous benchmarking as a service. The result is that no one actually knows how good anyone else is, or where the real frontier sits.

Good benchmarks require operating and maintaining physical hardware and real-world setups. Simulation only goes so far, since models that look strong in sim can show large performance gaps once deployed in the real world. Building real-world benchmarks means coordinating job-domain experts, evals engineering, and hands-on robotics all at once.

Frontier labs are targeting general-purpose robotics by 2028, yet the field of robotics evals barely exists. Whoever builds the trusted measure of robot capability becomes the reference everyone relies on. We combine backgrounds in AI evals and robotics to build and grow this field as fast as possible. We already shipped v1 of our open-source framework, Inspect Robots, and ran our first pilot scoring a frontier model on a real robot.
one_liner: Evals for robots

Previously Research Fellow at MATS, researcher at the UK AI Security Institute, and top contributor to Inspect Evals, the UK government's AI eval framework. Published at ACM EC, ICML, ACL, and EMNLP. Called the 2024 election correctly in all 50 states. Won a Rhodes Scholarship. Gold medal at the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics.

launches.title: Robocurve — Real-World Evaluations of Physical AI
launches.tagline: Real-world evals for robots
launches.body:
Hi, I’m [Jay](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeqcho/), co-founder of [Robocurve](http://robocurve.org). We measure and reports what frontier robots can actually do in the real world.

Our launch video <https://youtu.be/Cjkt2ikvsiQ>

Frontier labs are racing to build general-purpose robots within two years, yet no one knows what today's robots are truly capable of. Demo videos of robots performing narrow, cherry-picked tasks proliferate, but there are no rigorous, continuous, standardized benchmarks for robotics.

Robocurve builds benchmarks for robots and the AI models that control them, to help the world understand how far robotics has come and how fast it's moving. Our benchmarks range from playing Jenga and making a sandwich to constructing a data center.

General-purpose robots could arrive before the end of the decade, with far-reaching implications: accelerated data center buildouts, explosive economic growth from a fully automated economy, and intensified geopolitical competition between the US and China. Real-world evaluations from Robocurve will help clarify the timeline to general-purpose robots so that society can prepare for their arrival well ahead of time.

[Jay](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeqcho/) is a Rhodes Scholar and a top contributor to UK AI Security Institute's Inspect Evals. He has published papers in ICML, EMNLP, ACL, ACM EC and his research has been featured in MIT Technology Review. Previously, he spent time at AWS Bedrock, MATS, and Harvard where he completed his BA and MA with a highest honors thesis on AI and democracy.

If you build robots or AI models, reach out! We'd love to put them to the test. Learn more at [robocurve.org](http://robocurve.org).

launches.title: hardware intelligence: AI tools for the chips your AI runs on
launches.tagline: Bringing the $20B chip tooling industry into this decade
launches.body:
---

---

**Update:** We’ve just launched our second tool, WaveZip - a genuine breakthrough method for capturing and storing waveforms. Read more at <https://hardwareintelligence.ai/wavezip/>

---

---

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KJTH-nNl6qQ>

—

We’re Athreya and Rishov - the founders of [@hardware intelligence](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/company/33573). We’re here to pick a fight with the $20B industry whose debuggers suck and won’t open until an ancient license server gives it permission.

**TL;DR: Our first product, Wave, is a SOTA waveform debugger that lives completely in the terminal, built for the agentic era.** An agent can jump you to the moment a design breaks, drag in waveforms and manipulate them, trace bad signals to its source and even prove its fix against the simulation - all visual. We allow teams to build better chips in less time.

**The quick ask:** If you or anyone you know builds or verifies chips (ASICs/FPGAs), please email us! We would love to talk :)

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5nXvicwWONQ>

❌ **The Problem**

The AI boom is a chip boom - more companies and teams than ever are designing silicon. However, the reality is hardware is not software: you can’t patch a chip after it ships. A bug that reaches manufacturing can be a nine-figure mistake. That’s why **companies spend 70% of the entire chip design process just on verification**.

Hardware verification engineers run thousands of simulated tests first on their code (simulation) which typically can take **hours to days**. If one of these tests fail, debugging means reading a waveform - a log of every signal, millions of ticks long, hiding the tick where a value went wrong. It’s literally a needle in a haystack… a big haystack. It’s common for these waveform files to be several gigabytes large. **Finding this needle is the single largest activity in verification.**

**The current tools are dinosaurs.** 20-year-old GUIs behind license servers whose seats run six figures a year sold by our favorite incumbents: Synopsys, Cadence, and Siemens. Free tools are even worse.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=107661&key=user_uploads/551607/fd100b13-f0dd-45f0-8ee4-395edf96fcae)

Yes. This is from 2026.

Software engineers got coding agents. Chip engineers got a queue for a license and whatever this is.

👋 **What Wave actually does**

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=107661&key=user_uploads/551607/a75818b0-b001-466b-9586-705d26deb5f9)

Wave is the first of its kind! **A fully terminal-native waveform debugger with a verification agent built in.** Wave opens files before Verdi, the industry-standard viewer, finishes its license check. Let’s do a quick dive!

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=107661&key=user_uploads/551607/ac7e5c75-8abb-4a6d-881f-a2a9b883a8b3)

**Why the terminal?** Surprisingly, most hardware engineers are terminal power users - typically doing all their coding in Vim. We wanted to meet them where they are and make our product extremely intuitive to use - we even employ Vim bindings across the interface.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=107661&key=user_uploads/551607/d4063fbc-2f57-4b5c-a421-bfaa697433d6)

**Ask in plain english.** _Why is a wave x at 12.4us?_ The agent will pull in signals, act on them and trace the root cause. Everything happens in front of your eyes.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=107661&key=user_uploads/551607/8f37dd5c-22f0-4271-b665-a096c5dbfbd2)

**Pick your fix and see it.** Wave will propose different approaches with tradeoffs. The definition of “best” in hardware design depends on the use case. Maybe you want to optimize for performance? Maybe for power? Pick the one for you! Wave re-simulates and re-reads the new waveform. See a diff of how the waveform changed and a visual indication of where the fix was implemented.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=107661&key=user_uploads/551607/b0875bc9-fb55-4275-8c7e-11f926bc597d)

Now watch it fix a bug end to end with Rishov!

<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eTycCILW6Jk>

🙏 **Asks & Offers**

If you design chips or lead a team, email us! We’d love to work with you and speed up your RTL development.

Know someone who does? Email us!

Just want to chat about hardware? **EMAIL US!!**

👬 **The Team**

We met in our freshman dorm at Georgia Tech nearly a decade ago! We became best friends and roommates for all four years of college - after, Athreya went to NYC to work at Google and Rishov stayed to do his PhD. We promised each other that once we’re free, that we’ll go all-in and work on something we’re passionate about together. Turns out, Rishov’s deep PhD thesis on chip simulation and compilers was the perfect spark.

Today we announce our company and are roommates once again ❤️

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=107661&key=user_uploads/551607/eef30a82-c606-494a-a093-3649920c7857)

—

Say hi 👋 [hi@hardwareintelligence.ai](mailto:hi@hardwareintelligence.ai) · [hardwareintelligence.ai](http://hardwareintelligence.ai)

[@Athreya Anand](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/551607) · [athreya@hardwareintelligence.ai](mailto:athreya@hardwareintelligence.ai)

[@Rishov Sarkar](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/2565323) · [rishov@hardwareintelligence.ai](mailto:rishov@hardwareintelligence.ai)

P.S. Wave is just the start 👀 We got some super cool things coming to close the loop of hardware engineering.

name: Hemlock
long_description:
Every serious robotics lab is bottlenecked on the same thing: demonstration data. The field has converged on egocentric video and hand pose as the substrate, and both are now cheap to collect at scale. What neither of them contains is force. A video of someone picking up an egg and a video of someone picking up a rock are nearly identical in pixel space and nearly identical in joint angles. They differ almost entirely in a quantity nobody is recording. Policies trained without it learn geometry and inherit no sense of touch.

Hemlock closes that gap at the source. Our device, the Bracelet, is a wrist-worn surface EMG band that reads the electrical activity of the forearm muscles that actually drive the hand, which means it recovers contraction force directly rather than inferring it from motion. This distinction is the whole thesis: force cannot be reconstructed downstream of kinematics, because a hand squeezing hard isometrically and a hand resting can occupy the identical pose. Muscle signal is the only non-invasive channel that separates them.
one_liner: Force-sensing wristband for training robotic AI
